1.pericope_label: A good name is better than precious ointment, and the day of death than the day of one’s birth: it is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting: sorrow is better than laughter: the heart of the wise is in the house of mourning

schools.summary: Henry reads the ointment as a stand-in for the profits of the earth, the delights of sense and the highest titles of honour, since kings are anointed, and sets against them a name for wisdom and goodness among the wise and good, the memory of the just, which gives a larger opportunity of usefulness and outlasts the most precious box of ointment; he adds that Christ paid Mary for her ointment with a good name in the gospels and always pays with advantage.

Gill turns the good name into a divine name, reports that the third verse may be rendered anger rather than sorrow and that Jewish interpreters referred it to the anger of God in correcting men, better than his taking no notice and suffering them to go on as though he were pleased with them, citing the generation of the flood and the Sodomites, and observes that the wise man’s heart is in the house of mourning even when it does not suit him to go there in person.

Clarke sets out an argument of the whole chapter and then quotes eight lines of verse on the spotless name that is sweeter than fragrant balms; he notes that birthdays were kept with great festivity and holds that we seldom return from the house of feasting with one profitable thought or one solid impression; he says the sorrowful try themselves at the tribunal of their own consciences and resolve on amendment; and he calls the preference of the giddy for times of diversion, where they are kept from considering their latter end, the grand fault and misfortune of youth. Wesley prefers the day of death because this life is so full of vanity and vexation, and warns that feasting is attended with levity and manifold temptations.

Ellicott finds a play on words in the original, rendered by Plumptre as a good name being better than good nard, takes the line for an older proverb completed by the Preacher’s startling addition about the day of death, guards the book elsewhere as recommending not reckless enjoyment but enjoyment tempered by the fear of God, and allows that anger is the usual meaning of the word in the third verse though the context requires the received rendering. Keil and Delitzsch describe the house of mourning and its seven or thirty days, distinguish the mourning kept before burial from that kept after, call the book one standing on the border of both Testaments, and make the third verse a call for joy tempered with seriousness, since laughter only masks the disquiet peculiar to man.

debates: Is the third verse about sorrow or about anger? Gill and Ellicott both report that anger is the usual meaning of the word and that the older translators adopted it; Ellicott holds that the context requires the received rendering, and Gill passes on a Jewish reading of it as the corrective anger of God.

Is the first verse an original saying? Ellicott takes it for an older proverb which the Preacher completes with the startling addition about the day of death, and points to a play on words in the original.

How far does the book approve enjoyment? Ellicott sets this passage beside an earlier one and concludes that what is recommended there is not reckless enjoyment but enjoyment tempered by the fear of God.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch supply the mourning customs behind the second verse, seven days of lamentation and in some cases thirty, with a later distinction between the mourning before burial and the mourning after.
Clarke quotes eight lines of verse in place of a comment on the first verse, and prefaces the chapter with an argument of its contents.
Henry notes that Christ paid Mary for her ointment with a good name in the gospels.
themes: a name weighed against an ointment
the day of death preferred to the day of birth
what is learned in the house of mourning
sorrow or anger in the third verse
laughter as a mask for disquiet

5.pericope_label: It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise: as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool: surely oppression maketh a wise man mad: better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof

schools.summary: Henry grants the temptation of the seventh verse to be strong, since a wise man much and long oppressed is apt to speak and act unlike himself, to lay the reins on the neck of his passions and break out into indecent complaints, and he concludes that we should make great allowances for those who are ill dealt with and not be severe in censuring them, since we know not what we should do if the case were our own.

Gill presses the material of the thorns rather than the sound, weak and useless and fit only for burning, so that the loud laughter of a fool makes no melody; he says the rebuke of the wise shows the hearer wise as well as the giver; he allows both senses of the seventh verse, the wise man disturbed by oppression he sees or suffers and the wise man whose wisdom departs when he oppresses others; and he qualifies the eighth verse by the end of evil things before instancing the end of Job.

Clarke applies the crackling thorns to the joys of life, noisy and flashy and extinguished in a few moments; he refuses the received rendering of the seventh verse, since the root behind the verb means to glister and irradiate as well as to rage, so that oppression may be said to give lustre to a wise man, and he denies that a truly religious man can be driven mad by any oppression, since in patience he possesses his soul; and he answers the eighth verse with four lines of Byrom on the patient mind. Wesley makes the thorns a noise and blaze that presently go out, states the two ways a wise man may be made mad, by suffering oppression or by taking bribes to inflict it, and explains that the proud stands where we should expect the hasty because pride is the chief cause of impatience.

Ellicott reports the wordplay of the sixth verse as nettles under the kettle in German and as stubble that makes the pot bubble in Plumptre, would open the seventh verse with For rather than Surely since it stands in a series of paragraphs beginning with better, passes on Delitzsch’s conjecture that a line beginning with that word has dropped out, and holds that the man who commits the oppression rather than the man who suffers it is the one who goes mad; he also allows that the word rendered thing in the eighth verse may be rendered word. Keil and Delitzsch decline to explain the particle opening the seventh verse, render it that oppression maketh wise men mad and corruption destroyeth the understanding, take the subject to be the duties of a judge, define the oppression as forcing those who need legal help to buy it with presents, and qualify the eighth verse as untrue of a thing evil in itself, recalling Solon’s saying to Croesus.

debates: Who is made mad by oppression, the man who suffers it or the man who commits it? Ellicott says the one who commits it, Henry treats the sufferer, Gill and Wesley allow both, and Clarke denies the rendering altogether and would have oppression give lustre to a wise man.

Has a line dropped out of the seventh verse? Ellicott passes on Delitzsch’s conjecture that it once began with the word better, like the paragraphs around it, and offers as a milder remedy a connection through the rebuke of the wise.
Is the end always better than the beginning? Keil and Delitzsch deny it of a thing evil in itself, and Gill makes the same distinction between the end of wickedness and the end of good men.
outliers: Ellicott cites Delitzsch by name on the seventh verse, so that two of the voices in this set meet on the page.
Ellicott collects two attempts to keep the jingle of the sixth verse in translation, nettles under the kettle and stubble that makes the pot bubble.
Clarke twice answers a verse with poetry rather than exposition, quoting Byrom on the patient mind at the eighth verse.
themes: a blaze that is over before the pot boils
the rebuke that makes the hearer wise
oppression suffered or oppression done
a bribe that unseats the understanding
judging a thing by its end

9.pericope_label: Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry, for anger resteth in the bosom of fools: say not thou, what is the cause that the former days were better than these: wisdom is good with an inheritance

schools.summary: Henry turns the eleventh verse round, that an inheritance is good for little without wisdom, and finds wisdom good for the poor to make them content and good for the rich to keep them from being hurt by what they have, since an estate puts a man in a greater capacity of being useful.

Gill takes the anger of the ninth verse to be with men for every disagreeable word or else with God for his corrections, notes that men lay the blame for hard times on providence and murmur at it, and offers both renderings of the eleventh verse while observing that wisdom without riches is generally overlooked and despised, whereas wealth joined to wisdom commands attention and puts a man in a position to do good.

Clarke allows the wise man a moment of anger but denies it can rest in him, being a fire he casts out of his breast, while the fool fosters it into malice and revenge, whence come those dangerous and empty fools called duellists; he calls the complaint about the former days as foolish as it is common, since men were as wicked then and religion as unfashionable, and adds an eastern proverb that it is not the age that is corrupt but the men of the age; and he treats the eleventh verse as an objector’s interruption, since the book states objections in their full strength before combating them. Wesley makes the complaint about former days the mark of an unthankful mind and a contending of shallow wit with unsearchable wisdom.

Keil and Delitzsch make the hasty anger a form of pride, ask why the text says in thy spirit rather than soul or heart, and picture anger cherished in the bosom of fools as a wicked demon at home there; they quote two lines of Horace against the man who praises the times of his boyhood, and observe that the days meant include the years the speaker himself lived through; and they refuse to render the eleventh verse as good as an inheritance, holding that the thought is different from with an inheritance, that the distinction is not merely formal, and that the sense occurred to none of the ancient translators. Ellicott gives the ninth verse a bare cross reference, notes that the preposition of the tenth belongs to later Hebrew, and argues from two passages that the word of the eleventh will bear the marginal sense, as good as, which he thinks agrees better with the context.

debates: Is wisdom good with an inheritance or as good as one? Ellicott and Gill allow the marginal sense and Ellicott argues from two passages that the word will bear it, while Keil and Delitzsch insist the thought is different, the distinction not merely formal, and the sense unknown to the ancient translators.

Whose voice speaks in the eleventh verse? Clarke takes it for an objector interrupting, on the ground that the book states objections in their full strength before answering them, so that the wise man is not to be read as contradicting himself.
Why is the question about former days unwise? Keil and Delitzsch say it is not asked out of wisdom, Clarke denies the premise outright, and Wesley makes it a mark of ingratitude.
outliers: Clarke ends his note on anger with a remark on duellists, whom he calls a class of dangerous and empty fools.
Clarke quotes an eastern proverb that it is not the age that is corrupt but the men of the age.
Keil and Delitzsch personify anger as a wicked demon that feels itself at home in the bosom of fools.
themes: anger that lodges instead of passing
the former days and the flattering memory
a preposition worth an argument
wisdom and money as two shadows
the objector who interrupts the book

12.pericope_label: Wisdom is a defence, and money is a defence: consider the work of God: in the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider: be not righteous over much, neither make thyself over wise

schools.summary: Gill takes the defence for a shadow of refreshment and protection under which men sit with pleasure and safety, best of all when wisdom and money meet in the same man; he addresses the counsel to consider the work of God to those who quarrel with providence and says the work cannot be made better nor otherwise than it is; and he limits the warning against being righteous over much to the show and ostentation of righteousness, since a man cannot be too holy, naming the rigid and censorious temper that goes beyond the law, abstains from lawful things and macerates the body with fastings, pilgrimages and penance.

Clarke keeps up his dialogue, having the wise man answer that money supports animal life while wisdom gives life to those who have it and cannot procure the favour of God; he takes the crooked thing narrowly, since providence puts money into the hands of few while wisdom is within the reach of all; he says the sunshine will not last and that God has balanced prosperity against adversity, since otherwise many would put prosperity in the place of God; and he reads the fifteenth verse as another objection, marking where the speech ends and paraphrasing its drift, that there is no need of all this watching and fasting and self-denial. Wesley makes riches an exposure to destruction, offers the thirteenth verse as the last and best remedy against murmuring, finds the purpose of the alternation in keeping men dependent on God, and reads the warning as spoken in the person of an ungodly man.

Keil and Delitzsch call the thirteenth verse a proverb of devout submission to providence and gloss it as recognising the government of God in all that is done; they render the fourteenth as being of good cheer in the good day and observing in the day of misfortune, since God has made the one equal to the other; and they find the real difficulty of the sixteenth verse in its second half, since it is strange that the author should warn against an excess of wickedness as if a certain degree were advisable, and stranger that the contrast offered is folly rather than wickedness. Ellicott gives the literal shadow behind the word defence, takes the last clause of the fourteenth verse with the first so that a man should take the enjoyment God gives while he cannot tell what will come after him, and reads the warning as against morbid scrupulosity and over-rigorism, instancing those who refused to defend themselves on the sabbath.

debates: Who speaks the warning against being righteous over much? Clarke and Wesley both take it for an objector or an ungodly man rather than the wise man himself, while Gill and Ellicott keep it as counsel and limit it to ostentation and over-rigorism.

Why does the passage warn against excess of wickedness? Keil and Delitzsch call this the real difficulty, since it seems to allow a degree of wickedness, and note that the contrast offered is folly rather than wickedness.

What is the crooked thing that cannot be made straight? Clarke confines it to the distribution of money, which providence puts into the hands of few, while Gill and Wesley take it for the whole government of God, which no man can correct or alter.
outliers: Clarke marks in his own text where the objector’s speech ends and the wise man resumes, and paraphrases the objection in the language of his own day.
Ellicott illustrates over-rigorism from those who refused to defend themselves against their enemies on the sabbath.
Wesley explains the alternation of prosperity and adversity as designed to keep a man from foreseeing what will befall him, and so dependent on God.
themes: a shadow that money and wisdom both cast
submission as the cure for murmuring
the two days balanced against each other
righteousness that becomes ostentation
a warning that may be an objection

17.pericope_label: Be not over much wicked, neither be thou foolish: it is good that thou shouldest take hold of this: wisdom strengtheneth the wise more than ten mighty men which are in the city: there is not a just man upon earth that doeth good and sinneth not: take no heed unto all words that are spoken

schools.summary: Gill offers three ways of taking the warning against being over much wicked, as a caution to those emboldened by the long life of the wicked, as a warning against restless bustling after wealth on the original sense of the word, or as a warning against aggravating sin until a man despairs; he reads the eighteenth verse as advice to keep clear of extremes, makes wisdom a guard and a guide and hears behind it the wisdom of God, allows no exception to the twentieth verse but one and adds that the spirits of just men are made perfect in heaven, and advises a man not to inquire what is said of him but often to feign that he has not heard, lest by rehearsing a matter he store it up and meditate revenge.

Clarke reads the seventeenth verse as an instruction not to add opposition to godliness to the rest of one’s crimes, since perdition will come soon enough, and rebukes a learned doctor who preached three sermons on the text to show the sin, folly and danger of being righteous overmuch; he keeps a practical tone on the eighteenth verse, illustrates the strength of wisdom by Archimedes defending Syracuse against a fleet, insists that the twentieth verse says the just man may sin and not that he does, and calls the counsel about words much for every man’s peace through life while glossing the curse as making light of a man. Wesley reads the eighteenth verse as a promise of deliverance from all extremes and says only that one should not search into what is spoken.

Keil and Delitzsch render the close of the eighteenth verse as saying that he who fears God accomplishes both, reject the alternative that he escapes all and the supplement of all the perplexities of life, and prefer the results of the two extremes; they refuse to let the ten mighty men be multiplied indefinitely or made commanders of a garrison and suspect a definite political arrangement, perhaps ten archons; they trace the twentieth verse to the prayer at the consecration of the temple and note that the word for man stands for the species; and they refer the words of the twenty-first verse to the babbling of people in general rather than to talk about the reader. Ellicott makes the eighteenth verse a licence to try opposite rules of conduct under the fear of God, notes that the word for mighty men is elsewhere rendered governor, and confesses that only forced explanations have been given of the word opening the twentieth verse.

debates: What does the fearer of God escape or accomplish? Keil and Delitzsch render it that he accomplishes both extremes rightly, against the rendering that he escapes all, and against the supplement of all the perplexities of life.

Who are the ten mighty men? Keil and Delitzsch reject both an indefinite many and a garrison command, and suspect ten archons of a definite political arrangement; Ellicott notes the word is elsewhere rendered governor; Clarke drops the question for the example of Archimedes.

Whose words are not to be heeded? Keil and Delitzsch take them for the babbling of people at large rather than talk about the reader, since the text carries no restriction and a servant would have no cause to curse a master living by these maxims.
outliers: Clarke rebukes a learned doctor who preached three sermons on this text to prove the sin, folly and danger of being righteous overmuch, and says he out-did the infidel of the book itself.
Clarke illustrates the strength of one wise man by Archimedes at Syracuse, whose engines destroyed the fleet so that the city fell only by betrayal.
Ellicott admits that only forced explanations have been given of the connecting word that opens the twentieth verse.
themes: a warning that resists being taken as advice
holding one without letting go the other
one wise head against ten strong ones
the just man who may sin
the wisdom of not listening

22.pericope_label: For oftentimes also thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others: all this have I proved by wisdom: that which is far off, and exceeding deep, who can find it out: I applied mine heart to know, and to search, and to seek out wisdom

schools.summary: Henry says that here more than anywhere in the book the writer puts on the habit of a penitent, having had wisdom enough to see the vanity of the world and to learn that it makes no portion for a soul, but finding himself at a loss when he enquired further, his eye too dim and his line too short.

Gill calls the heart of the twenty-second verse the conscience, which is as a thousand witnesses; he acknowledges with the writer that all his wisdom fell short of perfection; he collects several senses of the far-off thing and passes on two scholars who read it that the image of God in man, which consisted in perfect wisdom, is now lost, which is why wisdom is far from him; and he says the search took in every corner.

Clarke asks who is free from evil speaking, from detailing a neighbour’s faults, from whispering and talebearing, and warns that a man should not wonder at being calumniated when he has so often calumniated others; he divides the question of the far-off thing, since the wisdom essential to salvation may be soon learned by the Spirit while wisdom itself has depths none can fathom; and he makes the twenty-fifth verse a warrant for enquiry, since a man with reason and understanding is called to use it as truly as he is called to believe, every doctrine of God being a subject for reason as well as faith, before adding six lines of verse on the wisdom that descends from heaven and the foul streams of folly. Wesley reports the writer determined to attain perfection of wisdom and greatly disappointed, and notes that three words are used for one thing to mark the vehemence of his desire.

Keil and Delitzsch define the wisdom sought as a complete wisdom that would adjust the contradictions of life, expound the mysteries of time and eternity and settle the weightiest questions, and compare the search of Job through every region of the world, which ended in the discovery that God has appointed man only a limited share; they refuse the rendering of the twenty-fourth verse that asks who can find out what is remote and deep, since the phrase is everywhere an idea complete in itself; and they report that almost all interpreters and the accentuation read I and my heart in the twenty-fifth, but call it so unpsychological an expression, and so without example, that many manuscripts read with my heart. Ellicott says the confession of failure gives energy to the practical lesson that follows, renders the twenty-fourth verse that which is, is far off, and notes that the noun for the reason of things is almost peculiar to this book, occurring elsewhere only in a plural meaning military engines.

debates: What is far off in the twenty-fourth verse? Keil and Delitzsch refuse the rendering that makes it simply what is remote and deep, holding that the phrase means what has been or what has come into existence; Ellicott renders it that which is, is far off and takes it for the constitution of the universe; Gill passes on a reading that finds the lost image of God in it.

Did the writer turn himself and his heart, or turn with his heart? Keil and Delitzsch note that the accentuation and almost all interpreters take the first, but call the expression unpsychological and without example, and prefer the reading of many manuscripts.

How far may reason be used? Clarke makes the search of the twenty-fifth verse a duty, since a man is called to use his understanding as truly as to believe, and calls the man who neglects it a slothful servant.
outliers: Ellicott notes that the noun rendered the reason of things occurs elsewhere only in a plural that means military engines.
Keil and Delitzsch compare the failed search of this passage with the search of Job through every region of the world and among all creatures.
Clarke answers the twenty-fifth verse with six lines of verse on the fountain of living waters and the foul streams of folly.
themes: conscience as a thousand witnesses
a confession of failure in wisdom
the far-off thing and what it names
a circuit drawn around the knowable
reason called to work as faith is

26.pericope_label: I find more bitter than death the woman whose heart is snares and nets: behold, this have I found, counting one by one: one man among a thousand have I found: God hath made man upright, but they have sought out many inventions

schools.summary: Gill states at once that the woman of the twenty-sixth verse is not the sex in general, which he says the writer had no intention of reproaching, but the adulterous woman whose snares bring painful and scandalous diseases and a horror into the awakened conscience; he says only of the search that it was made with great intenseness and did not succeed; and he insists that the making upright covers both of the first pair, created the same day and in the same image, and describes not the erectness of their bodies but the disposition of their minds.

Clarke finds nothing in the whole enquiry so dangerous as the blandishments of cunning women, since when the affections are entangled escape is almost impossible, and notes that the figure is drawn from a hunting party with nets and gins; he describes the counting as a comparison of wisdom with wiles and reason with arts, calls the result a lamentable account of the morals of that country and time, and thanks God that a tithe of both could be found in his own day; he passes on a paraphrase that turns the verse into a hunt for one perfect man from the first man to the patriarch, found among the thousand kings who built the tower; and he lays out four renderings of the closing words before doubting that the word should be taken in a bad sense at all, since it may cover the arts and sciences and schemes that God gave men faculties to produce. Wesley makes the escape a being kept from falling into her hands, takes the thousand for the company the writer had drawn into his own society, and says that though the streams of wickedness could not all be traced the fountain was discovered, the corruption of nature that is in men and women alike.

Keil and Delitzsch hold that two words of the twenty-seventh verse should be divided differently, following the form the phrase takes near the end of the book, and report Ginsburg disputing this on the ground that the name for the preacher may be feminine as well as masculine, and another scholar supposing the feminine deliberate, as true wisdom set against false philosophy, which they reject; and they call the statement that God made man upright dogmatically significant, since man as he came from the Creator’s hand was not set in a state of moral decision nor in indifference between good and evil, but was normal in every respect and able to develop from a positively good foundation. Ellicott observes that a disparaging estimate of the female sex is common in countries where polygamy is practised, allows that a man with a thousand wives might not find a good one among them, and sets three passages of another book against the conclusion.

debates: How should the twenty-seventh verse be divided? Keil and Delitzsch redivide two words after the form the phrase takes near the end of the book; Ginsburg disputes it, holding the name for the preacher may be feminine, and another scholar takes the feminine as deliberate.

Is the estimate of women in this passage to be accepted? Gill restricts it to the adulterous woman, Ellicott traces it to the practice of polygamy and cites three passages against it, and Clarke calls it a lamentable account of the morals of that place and time.

Are the many inventions a fault? Clarke doubts the word should be taken in a bad sense at all, since it may cover the arts and sciences and schemes that human faculties have produced, while Wesley reads the whole line as the discovery of the fountain of wickedness.
outliers: Clarke passes on a paraphrase that turns the search into a hunt for one perfect man among the thousand kings who built the tower, and for a woman like the patriarch’s wife among their wives.
Ellicott sets three passages of another book against the conclusion drawn here about women.
Clarke collects four renderings of the closing words, from meddling with endless questions to seeking divers subtleties.
themes: a warning restricted to one kind of woman
a count that reflects on the counter
a name that may be feminine
man made normal, not neutral
inventions as fault or as faculty
